nodes.name: Cook–Levin theorem
nodes.statement: The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-complete: it is in NP, and every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time.
nodes.by: Stephen Cook, 1971, and independently Leonid Levin, 1973
nodes.note: SAT was the first problem shown to be NP-complete. Every later NP-completeness proof starts from it, directly or through a chain of reductions.

nodes.name: Karp's 21 NP-complete problems
nodes.statement: Twenty-one classic combinatorial problems, among them clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian circuit, chromatic number and max cut, are NP-complete.
nodes.by: Richard Karp, 1972
nodes.note: Karp gave polynomial-time reductions from SAT to each problem, directly or through a chain of his other reductions, so the list rests on Cook's theorem.

nodes.name: Deterministic time hierarchy theorem
nodes.statement: For every time-constructible bound f(n) there is a problem that can be solved in time O(f(n) log f(n)) but not in time o(f(n)). More time lets a computer solve strictly more problems.
nodes.by: Juris Hartmanis and Richard E. Stearns, 1965; the log-factor form stated here uses the faster universal simulation of Fred Hennie and Stearns, 1966

nodes.name: P is strictly contained in EXPTIME
nodes.statement: Some problems that can be solved in exponential time cannot be solved in polynomial time.
nodes.by: Corollary of the time hierarchy theorem of Hartmanis and Stearns, 1965
nodes.note: One of the few separations between natural complexity classes that is actually proven. It follows by applying the hierarchy theorem to two exponential time bounds.

nodes.name: P ≠ NP
nodes.statement: Some problems whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time cannot be solved in polynomial time. Equivalently, no NP-complete problem, such as SAT, Hamiltonian circuit or the travelling salesman decision problem, has a polynomial-time algorithm.
nodes.by: Stated precisely by Stephen Cook, 1971, and independently by Leonid Levin, 1973
nodes.note: A Clay Millennium Prize Problem. Each of NP ≠ co-NP and the existence of one-way functions would imply it. The converses are not known.

nodes.name: NP ≠ co-NP
nodes.statement: The classes NP and co-NP are different. Equivalently, there is no system of certificates of polynomial length, checkable in polynomial time, that proves every tautology of propositional logic.
nodes.by: Implicit in Cook, 1971; the proof-system form is due to Stephen Cook and Robert Reckhow, 1979
nodes.note: Because P is closed under complement, P = NP would force NP = co-NP. So NP ≠ co-NP implies P ≠ NP. Deciding whether a formula is a tautology is co-NP-complete.

nodes.name: Ladner's theorem
nodes.statement: There are problems in NP that are neither solvable in polynomial time nor NP-complete.
nodes.by: Richard E. Ladner, 1975
nodes.note: Ladner proved that such NP-intermediate problems exist if P ≠ NP. Natural candidates are graph isomorphism and the decision versions of factoring and discrete logarithm.

nodes.name: PCP theorem
nodes.statement: Every problem in NP has proofs that a randomized checker can verify by reading only a constant number of bits of the proof, using O(log n) random bits: NP = PCP[O(log n), O(1)].
nodes.by: Sanjeev Arora and Shmuel Safra; Sanjeev Arora, Carsten Lund, Rajeev Motwani, Madhu Sudan and Mario Szegedy, 1992 (journal versions 1998)
nodes.note: Equivalent to saying that approximating the fraction of satisfiable constraints of a constraint problem within some constant factor is NP-hard. Irit Dinur found a much simpler proof in 2005.

nodes.name: Raz's parallel repetition theorem
nodes.statement: Running a two-prover one-round proof system many times in parallel makes the probability that the verifier is fooled shrink exponentially in the number of repetitions, provided a single run fools the verifier with probability less than 1.
nodes.by: Ran Raz, 1998
nodes.note: The rate depends only on the original error and, logarithmically, on the number of possible answers. Combined with the PCP theorem it gives the starting point for sharp hardness-of-approximation results.

nodes.name: Håstad's optimal inapproximability of MAX-3SAT
nodes.statement: No polynomial-time algorithm can guarantee to satisfy a fraction 7/8 + ε of the clauses that the best assignment satisfies in formulas with exactly three literals per clause, for any ε > 0. A random assignment already satisfies 7/8 on average.
nodes.by: Johan Håstad, 2001 (conference version 1997)
nodes.note: What Håstad proved outright is that doing better than 7/8 + ε is NP-hard; that rules out an algorithm only if P ≠ NP. His proof starts from the PCP theorem combined with Raz's parallel repetition theorem.

nodes.name: IP = PSPACE
nodes.statement: The problems that have interactive proofs, in which a polynomial-time randomized verifier questions an all-powerful prover, are exactly the problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory.
nodes.by: Adi Shamir, 1992, using the technique of Carsten Lund, Lance Fortnow, Howard Karloff and Noam Nisan, 1990
nodes.note: Lund, Fortnow, Karloff and Nisan first gave interactive proofs for the permanent, and hence for co-NP and the whole polynomial hierarchy. Shamir extended their technique to all of PSPACE.

nodes.name: Strong exponential time hypothesis
nodes.statement: For every ε > 0 there is a k such that k-SAT on n variables cannot be solved in time 2^((1 − ε)n). Brute force over all assignments cannot be beaten by a constant factor in the exponent.
nodes.by: Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, 1999; stated in this form by Chris Calabro, Impagliazzo and Paturi, 2009
nodes.note: SETH implies ETH. So if the October 2026 claimed refutations of ETH are correct, SETH is false too.

nodes.name: Exponential time hypothesis
nodes.statement: 3-SAT on n variables cannot be solved in subexponential time 2^o(n).
nodes.by: Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, 1999
nodes.note: Many lower bounds for exact algorithms are proven assuming it.
nodes.claim: On 26 October 2026 OpenAI and Anthropic each released a claimed refutation: algorithms that count the satisfying assignments of 3-CNF formulas in time 2^O(n log log n / √log n), with Lean formalizations. OpenAI's Lean proof gives only the weaker 2^O(n (log log n)² / √log n). As of November 2026 neither has completed academic review. If either holds, this hypothesis and the strong form are false.

nodes.name: ETH lower bounds for NP-hard graph problems
nodes.statement: Graph k-colourability for each fixed k ≥ 3, Hamiltonian cycle, maximum clique, maximum independent set and vertex cover cannot be solved in time 2^o(n) on graphs with n vertices.
nodes.by: Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Francis Zane, 2001
nodes.note: Proven assuming ETH, using the sparsification lemma. The October 2026 claims would refute ETH. The MIT Hardness Group (2026) shows that the same reductions still rule out 2^(n^(1−ε)) algorithms under the weaker Stearns–Hunt hypothesis.

nodes.name: Orthogonal vectors conjecture
nodes.statement: For no ε > 0 can an algorithm decide in time N^(2 − ε)·poly(D) whether a set of N binary vectors of dimension D contains two orthogonal vectors.
nodes.by: Ryan Williams, 2005
nodes.note: Williams showed that a faster algorithm for orthogonal vectors would give a faster algorithm for SAT, so SETH implies this conjecture. Many quadratic lower bounds in fine-grained complexity are reductions from it. If SETH falls, this conjecture is not known to be affected.

nodes.name: Quadratic lower bound for edit distance (Backurs–Indyk)
nodes.statement: No algorithm computes the edit distance between two strings of length n in time O(n^(2 − δ)) for any constant δ > 0.
nodes.by: Arturs Backurs and Piotr Indyk, 2015
nodes.note: They reduce orthogonal vectors to edit distance, so a faster algorithm would break the orthogonal vectors conjecture and hence SETH. The textbook dynamic program takes about n² steps, so it would be essentially optimal.

nodes.name: Unique games conjecture
nodes.statement: For all small ε, δ > 0 there is a number of colours k such that, for constraint problems where each constraint between two variables fixes one variable's colour given the other's, it is NP-hard to tell apart instances where a 1 − δ fraction of constraints can be satisfied from instances where at most an ε fraction can.
nodes.by: Subhash Khot, 2002
nodes.note: If true, it pins down exactly how well many optimisation problems can be approximated.
nodes.claim: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI released an AI-written manuscript claiming a proof. The same release included a Lean-verified proof of the related 2-to-1 conjecture, which is a different statement. As of November 2026 neither has been independently reviewed.

nodes.name: 2-to-2 games theorem
nodes.statement: For 2-to-2 games, constraint problems in which each rule allows two choices for one variable for each choice of the other, it is NP-hard to tell apart instances where almost all rules can be satisfied from instances where only a small fraction can.
nodes.by: Subhash Khot, Dor Minzer and Muli Safra, with Irit Dinur and Guy Kindler on two of the four papers, 2018
nodes.note: It gives the unique games hardness for instances where about half the rules can be satisfied. The full conjecture needs instances where nearly all can.

nodes.name: Goemans–Williamson algorithm for MAX-CUT
nodes.statement: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm based on semidefinite programming finds, in any graph, a cut whose expected size is at least about 0.878 times the size of the largest cut.
nodes.by: Michel Goemans and David P. Williamson, 1995
nodes.note: Without the unique games conjecture, the best known hardness is that approximating max cut better than 16/17 ≈ 0.941 is NP-hard.

nodes.name: Majority is stablest theorem
nodes.statement: Among Boolean functions with mean zero in which no single input has much influence, majority is asymptotically the most noise-stable, for every fixed correlation between 0 and 1.
nodes.by: Elchanan Mossel, Ryan O'Donnell and Krzysztof Oleszkiewicz, 2005
nodes.note: Conjectured by Khot, Kindler, Mossel and O'Donnell for their MAX-CUT result, then proven through an invariance principle for low-influence polynomials.

nodes.name: Optimality of Goemans–Williamson under the unique games conjecture
nodes.statement: No polynomial-time algorithm approximates MAX-CUT within any factor better than the Goemans–Williamson ratio of about 0.878.
nodes.by: Subhash Khot, Guy Kindler, Elchanan Mossel and Ryan O'Donnell, 2004 (journal 2007)
nodes.note: They reduce unique games to approximating MAX-CUT within 0.878 + ε, so the bound holds if the unique games conjecture holds and P ≠ NP. The reduction relies on the majority is stablest theorem.

nodes.name: Vertex cover is hard to approximate within 2 − ε
nodes.statement: No polynomial-time algorithm approximates minimum vertex cover within any constant factor smaller than 2. A simple greedy matching algorithm achieves factor 2.
nodes.by: Subhash Khot and Oded Regev, 2003
nodes.note: Proven assuming the unique games conjecture. Without it, the best known NP-hardness factor is √2 − ε, from the 2-to-2 games theorem (Khot, Minzer and Safra, 2018).

nodes.name: Existence of one-way functions
nodes.statement: There is a function that is easy to compute but hard to invert: given f(x) for a random x, every polynomial-time algorithm finds a preimage only with negligible probability.
nodes.by: Basic open conjecture of cryptography
nodes.note: Their existence would prove P ≠ NP, but P ≠ NP is not known to imply it. Hard factoring gives one: the Rabin function is one-way if and only if factoring is hard.

nodes.name: Goldreich–Levin theorem
nodes.statement: If f is a one-way function, then from f(x) and a random string r nobody can efficiently predict the inner product of x and r modulo 2 noticeably better than by guessing.
nodes.by: Oded Goldreich and Leonid Levin, 1989
nodes.note: This gives every one-way function, after a trivial change, a hard-core bit. Hard-core bits are how pseudorandom bits are extracted from one-way functions.

nodes.name: Pseudorandom generators from any one-way function
nodes.statement: Pseudorandom generators exist: efficient functions that stretch a short random seed into a longer string that no efficient algorithm can tell apart from a truly random one.
nodes.by: Johan Håstad, Russell Impagliazzo, Leonid Levin and Michael Luby, 1999
nodes.note: They build a pseudorandom generator from any one-way function, using the Goldreich–Levin hidden bit. Since the converse is easy, pseudorandom generators exist if and only if one-way functions do.

nodes.name: Digital signatures from any one-way function
nodes.statement: Digital signature schemes secure against adaptive chosen-message attacks exist.
nodes.by: John Rompel, 1990
nodes.note: Rompel built universal one-way hash functions from any one-way function; Naor and Yung had shown these give secure signatures. Katz and Koo found errors in the original paper and published a complete proof in 2005.

nodes.name: Hardness of integer factoring
nodes.statement: No classical polynomial-time algorithm factors the product of two large random primes of similar size, except with negligible probability.
nodes.by: Long-standing assumption of public-key cryptography
nodes.note: No polynomial-time classical algorithm is known; the best is the general number field sieve. Factoring is in NP ∩ co-NP, so it is not expected to be NP-complete.

nodes.name: RSA assumption
nodes.statement: Given N = pq for random large primes p and q, a public exponent e coprime to (p−1)(q−1), and c = m^e mod N for a random m, no polynomial-time algorithm recovers m except with negligible probability.
nodes.by: Named after the cryptosystem of Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, 1977
nodes.note: Factoring N breaks RSA, so this assumption implies that factoring is hard. The reverse is not proven: breaking RSA might be easier than factoring, and Boneh and Venkatesan (1998) gave evidence in that direction.

nodes.name: Security of the Rabin function
nodes.statement: Extracting square roots modulo N = pq, that is, inverting x ↦ x² mod N for a random x, is infeasible.
nodes.by: Michael O. Rabin, 1979
nodes.note: Unlike RSA, Rabin's scheme is proven exactly as hard as factoring: anyone who can decrypt random ciphertexts can factor N.

nodes.name: Shor's algorithm
nodes.statement: A quantum computer can find the prime factors of an integer in time polynomial in its number of digits.
nodes.by: Peter Shor, 1994
nodes.note: The hardness of factoring is therefore an assumption about classical computers only. A large enough quantum computer would break RSA.

nodes.name: Worst-case quantum hardness of lattice problems
nodes.statement: No polynomial-time quantum algorithm solves the worst-case lattice problems GapSVP and SIVP within the polynomial approximation factors used in Regev's reduction.
nodes.by: Standard assumption of lattice-based cryptography
nodes.note: Regev's paper bases the security of its cryptosystem on this worst-case quantum hardness, through the learning with errors problem.

nodes.name: Hardness of learning with errors
nodes.statement: Given many random linear equations modulo q in a secret vector s, each off by a small random error, no polynomial-time algorithm can recover s, for suitable parameters (q polynomial in n, Gaussian errors of width at least 2√n).
nodes.by: Oded Regev, 2005 (journal 2009)
nodes.note: Regev proved, by a quantum reduction, that an efficient algorithm for LWE would give a quantum algorithm for GapSVP and SIVP. Peikert gave a classical reduction in 2009 from a non-standard variant of GapSVP.

nodes.name: Security of Regev's public-key encryption
nodes.statement: Regev's public-key encryption scheme, in which ciphertexts are noisy linear equations, is secure against chosen-plaintext attacks: no polynomial-time algorithm can tell an encryption of 0 from one of 1.
nodes.by: Oded Regev, 2005
nodes.note: The scheme is entirely classical. Its security proof assumes LWE is hard, and through Regev's reduction rests on the quantum hardness of worst-case lattice problems.

nodes.name: Exponential circuit lower bound for E
nodes.statement: Some problem solvable in time 2^O(n) requires Boolean circuits of size 2^Ω(n).
nodes.by: Hypothesis used by Russell Impagliazzo and Avi Wigderson, 1997

nodes.name: BPP = P
nodes.statement: Every problem that a randomized polynomial-time algorithm solves with small error probability can also be solved by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.
nodes.by: Russell Impagliazzo and Avi Wigderson, 1997
nodes.note: Proven assuming exponential circuit lower bounds for E, and widely conjectured on its own. Primality testing, long known to be in BPP, was shown to be in P unconditionally by Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena in 2002.

nodes.name: Babai's quasipolynomial algorithm for graph isomorphism
nodes.statement: Whether two graphs with n vertices are isomorphic can be decided in quasipolynomial time 2^O((log n)^c) for a fixed constant c.
nodes.by: László Babai, 2015 (claim restored after a correction in January 2017)
nodes.note: Graph isomorphism is a leading candidate for an NP-intermediate problem: it is not known to be in P, and Schöning showed in 1987 that it is not NP-complete unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses.

nodes.name: Entscheidungsproblem
nodes.statement: There is no algorithm that takes any statement of first-order logic and answers "yes" or "no" according to whether it is universally valid, that is, valid in every structure. This holds under the assumption that effectively calculable means computable by a Turing machine (the Church–Turing thesis).
nodes.by: Posed by David Hilbert and Wilhelm Ackermann, 1928; shown impossible by Alonzo Church and Alan Turing, 1936
nodes.note: By the completeness theorem of first-order logic, it is equivalent to asking for an algorithm that decides whether a statement is provable.

nodes.name: Bekić's theorem
nodes.statement: Let f: P × Q → P and g: P × Q → Q be operators on pointed directed-complete partial orders P and Q, continuous in each component. Then the least fixed point of (x, y) ↦ (f(x, y), g(x, y)) is the pair (x₀, y₀) with x₀ = μx. f(x, μy. g(x, y)) and y₀ = μy. g(x₀, y), where μ denotes the least fixed point in one variable.
nodes.by: Hans Bekić, 1969; published posthumously in a book by Cliff Jones, 1984
nodes.note: It allows a mutual recursion to be split into recursions on one variable at a time. A variant for complete lattices needs the operators only to be monotone.

nodes.name: Friedberg–Muchnik theorem
nodes.statement: There exist two computably enumerable languages A and B that are incomparable: there is no Turing reduction from A to B and none from B to A.
nodes.by: Albert Muchnik and Richard Friedberg, independently, in the middle of the 1950s
nodes.note: It strengthens the Kleene–Post theorem, which gives incomparable languages that are Turing reducible to the halting problem. Its proof is notable for the priority finite injury method.

nodes.name: No low-energy trivial state conjecture
nodes.statement: There is a family of local Hamiltonians H⁽ⁿ⁾ on n qubits, for infinitely many n, with the following properties. Each H⁽ⁿ⁾ is a sum of terms that each act on a bounded number of qubits and have bounded norm, each qubit is involved in a bounded number of terms, and each H⁽ⁿ⁾ has ground energy 0. There are also a constant ε > 0 and a function f such that every state U|0ⁿ⟩ prepared by a depth-d circuit U of two-qubit gates has energy ⟨0ⁿ|U†H⁽ⁿ⁾U|0ⁿ⟩ > εn whenever n ≥ f(d).
nodes.by: Conjectured by Michael Freedman and Matthew Hastings, 2013; proved by Anurag Anshu, Nikolas Breuckmann and Chinmay Nirkhe, 2023
nodes.note: It was intended as a weaker consequence of the conjectural quantum PCP theorem that would be easier to prove. The proof constructs Hamiltonians whose ground states are the codewords of a quantum stabilizer code.

nodes.name: Richardson's theorem
nodes.statement: Take expressions generated by the rational numbers, π, ln 2, the variable x, addition, subtraction, multiplication, composition, and the functions sin, exp and abs. There is no algorithm that decides whether such an expression is zero everywhere, so equality of the real numbers they define is undecidable. There is also no algorithm that decides whether such an expression is nonnegative everywhere.
nodes.by: Daniel Richardson, 1968
nodes.note: For some classes of expressions built from other primitives, algorithms exist that can decide whether an expression is zero.

nodes.name: Sensitivity theorem
nodes.statement: For every Boolean function f from {0,1}ⁿ to {0,1}, the sensitivity s(f) is at least the square root of the degree deg(f). Here deg(f) is the degree of the unique multilinear real polynomial expressing f, and s(f) is the largest number of coordinates whose flip changes the value of f at a single point.
nodes.by: Hao Huang, 2019; it settled a conjecture posed by Nisan and Szegedy in 1992
nodes.note: The bound is tight for the AND-of-ORs function, which has degree m² and sensitivity m.

nodes.name: Selman's theorem
nodes.statement: A set A is enumeration-reducible to a set B if and only if, for every oracle X, A is computably enumerable with oracle X whenever B is computably enumerable with oracle X.
nodes.by: Alan Selman, 1971, as part of his PhD thesis
nodes.note: It relates enumeration reducibility with enumerability relative to oracles.

nodes.name: Church–Rosser theorem
nodes.statement: In the pure untyped lambda calculus, if a term M reduces by β-reduction (in any number of steps, possibly none) to both N₁ and N₂, then there is a term X to which both N₁ and N₂ reduce. The same holds for η-reduction and for βη-reduction.
nodes.by: Alonzo Church and J. Barkley Rosser, 1936, for β-reduction in the λI-calculus; for the pure untyped lambda calculus, D. E. Schroer, 1965
nodes.note: The theorem means the reduction rules of the lambda calculus are confluent. As a consequence, a term has at most one normal form.

nodes.name: Borodin–Trakhtenbrot gap theorem
nodes.statement: For a fixed Turing machine model and any total computable function g with g(n) > n for all n, there is a total computable function t such that the functions computable in time t(n) are exactly those computable in time g(t(n)). So adding compute time need not allow more functions to be computed.
nodes.by: Proved independently by Boris Trakhtenbrot and Allan Borodin
nodes.note: It holds for any abstract (Blum) complexity measure. Because the bound t may be very large and nonconstructible, it says nothing about classes such as P or NP and does not contradict the time hierarchy theorem.

nodes.name: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
nodes.statement: If a real number x has an expansion in some base b ≥ 2 that is real-time computable, then x is rational or transcendental. An infinite word is real-time computable when a multitape Turing machine, run without input, writes its successive letters taking a bounded amount of time between two successive letters.
nodes.by: Juris Hartmanis and Richard E. Stearns, 1965
nodes.note: The conjecture would imply that there is no integer multiplication algorithm running in time O(n). Boris Adamczewski and Yann Bugeaud proved the case where the expansion is an automatic sequence.

nodes.name: Greibach's theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a class of formal languages over an alphabet Σ∪{#} such that each language in C has a finite description, every regular language over Σ∪{#} is in C, descriptions of L₁R, RL₁ and L₁∪L₂ can be computed effectively from descriptions of L₁, L₂ in C and a regular language R, and it is undecidable for a language L in C with L ⊆ Σ* whether L = Σ*. Let P be any nontrivial subset of C that contains all regular sets over Σ∪{#} and is closed under quotient by each single symbol in Σ∪{#}. Then it is undecidable, given a description of a language L in C, whether L belongs to P.
nodes.by: Sheila Greibach, 1963
nodes.note: It shows, for example, that it is undecidable whether a given context-free grammar describes a regular language.

nodes.name: Myhill isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: Two sets A, B ⊆ ℕ are computably isomorphic, meaning there is a computable bijection f: ℕ → ℕ with x ∈ A if and only if f(x) ∈ B, exactly when A is one-one reducible to B and B is one-one reducible to A. A one-one reduction is an injective total computable function f with x ∈ A if and only if f(x) ∈ B.
nodes.by: Named after John Myhill
nodes.note: It is reminiscent of the Schröder–Bernstein theorem in set theory and has been called a constructive version of it.

nodes.name: Blum's speedup theorem
nodes.statement: For any Blum complexity measure and any total computable function f of two parameters, there is a total computable predicate g such that for every program i computing g there is a program j computing g with f(x, Φⱼ(x)) ≤ Φᵢ(x) for almost all x. So some computable functions have no optimal program, because every program has a program of lower complexity.
nodes.by: Manuel Blum, 1967
nodes.note: The speedup function f may grow as fast as desired, so the smaller program can be significantly faster, for instance exponentially so.

nodes.name: Smn theorem
nodes.statement: Let m and n be positive integers. For every Turing machine TMₓ of arity m + n and all input values y₁, …, yₘ, there is a Turing machine TMₖ of arity n such that TMₓ(y₁, …, yₘ, z₁, …, zₙ) = TMₖ(z₁, …, zₙ) for all z₁, …, zₙ. Moreover, k can be computed from x and y₁, …, yₘ by a primitive recursive function Sᵐₙ.
nodes.by: Stephen Cole Kleene, 1938
nodes.note: In practical terms, there is an algorithm that takes the source code of a program with m + n free variables and m values, and produces code that substitutes those values for the first m variables.

nodes.name: Ogden's lemma
nodes.statement: If a language L is context-free, then there is a number p ≥ 1 such that the following holds for every string s in L of length at least p and every way of marking at least p positions of s. The string s can be written as s = uvwxy, where vx contains at least one marked position, vwx contains at most p marked positions, and uvⁿwxⁿy is in L for every n ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Named after William F. Ogden
nodes.note: When every position is marked it is equivalent to the pumping lemma for context-free languages. It can show that some languages are not context-free where the pumping lemma is not enough, and it can prove that some languages are inherently ambiguous.

nodes.name: Rice's theorem
nodes.statement: Let φ be an admissible numbering of the partial computable functions, and let P be a set of natural numbers that is neither empty nor all of ℕ and that is extensional: if φ_m = φ_n, then m is in P exactly when n is in P. Then P is undecidable. In words, every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable.
nodes.by: Henry Gordon Rice, 1951, in his doctoral dissertation at Syracuse University
nodes.note: The theorem generalizes the undecidability of the halting problem. It implies that no tool can check whether any given program is correct.

nodes.name: Kleene's recursion theorem
nodes.statement: Fix an admissible numbering φ of the partial recursive functions, where φₑ is the function with index e. For every partial recursive function Q(x, y) there is an index p such that, for every y, φₚ(y) and Q(p, y) are either both undefined or both defined and equal.
nodes.by: Stephen Kleene, 1938
nodes.note: This is the second recursion theorem. Rogers's fixed-point theorem is a simpler version of it. Taking Q(x, y) = x gives a program that outputs its own index, which is called a quine.

nodes.name: Mahaney's theorem
nodes.statement: If any sparse language is NP-hard, then P = NP.
nodes.by: Stephen Mahaney
nodes.note: It was motivated by the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture. It shows that, if P ≠ NP, there are no NP-complete sparse sets.

nodes.name: Fagin's theorem
nodes.statement: A property of finite structures, such as finite graphs, can be expressed in existential second-order logic exactly when it belongs to the complexity class NP. So the properties expressible in existential second-order logic are precisely the class NP.
nodes.by: Ronald Fagin, 1973, in his doctoral thesis; published in his 1974 paper
nodes.note: It is the oldest result of descriptive complexity theory. For example, 3-colorability of a graph can be written as an existential second-order formula.

nodes.name: Pumping lemma for regular languages
nodes.statement: For every regular language L there is an integer p ≥ 1, depending only on L, such that every string w in L of length at least p can be written as w = xyz with |y| ≥ 1 and |xy| ≤ p, and such that xyⁿz is in L for every n ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott, 1959; rediscovered by Yehoshua Bar-Hillel, Micha A. Perles and Eli Shamir, 1961
nodes.note: It is used to prove that a specific language is not regular, by showing that the language does not have this property. The converse is false: some non-regular languages also satisfy it.

nodes.name: No free lunch theorem for search and optimization
nodes.statement: Let X be a finite set of candidate solutions and Y a finite ordered set of cost values, and let the objective function from X to Y not change during the search. If every such function is equally likely, then for every m the probability of observing a given sequence of m cost values is the same for every deterministic search algorithm that never evaluates the same candidate twice.
nodes.by: David Wolpert and William G. Macready
nodes.note: Before Wolpert's article was published, Cullen Schaffer independently proved a restricted version of one of Wolpert's theorems. Later work showed that there is no free lunch exactly when the distribution of objective functions is unchanged by permuting the candidate solutions.

nodes.name: Pumping lemma for context-free languages
nodes.statement: If a language L is context-free, then there is an integer p ≥ 1 such that every string s in L of length at least p can be split as s = uvwxy, where v and x together contain at least one symbol (|vx| ≥ 1), |vwx| ≤ p, and uvⁿwxⁿy is in L for every n ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Named after Bar-Hillel
nodes.note: It is used to show by contradiction that a specific language is not context-free. It does not guarantee that a language is context-free: some languages that are not context-free still satisfy it.

nodes.name: Structured program theorem
nodes.statement: Every computable function can be computed by a flowchart (control-flow graph) that combines subprograms using only three control structures: sequence (run one subprogram, then another), selection (run one of two subprograms depending on a true or false test) and iteration (repeat a subprogram while a test is true). Such a program may need extra variables to keep track of information that the original program records by its position in the code.
nodes.by: Corrado Böhm, 1964 (sequence and iteration suffice); typically credited to the 1966 paper of Böhm and Jacopini
nodes.note: It is the basis of structured programming, which avoids the goto statement. Böhm's 1964 result says every partial recursive function can be computed using only sequence and iteration.

nodes.name: Post's theorem
nodes.statement: For every natural number n, a set B of natural numbers is Σ⁰ₙ₊₁ (a level of the arithmetical hierarchy) if and only if B can be computably enumerated by an oracle Turing machine with an oracle for ∅⁽ⁿ⁾, the n-fold iterated Turing jump of the empty set. Moreover, for every n > 0, ∅⁽ⁿ⁾ is Σ⁰ₙ-complete: every Σ⁰ₙ set is many-one reducible to ∅⁽ⁿ⁾.
nodes.by: Named after Emil Post
nodes.note: It connects the arithmetical hierarchy with the Turing degrees of the form ∅⁽ⁿ⁾. A corollary is that a set is arithmetical if and only if it is Turing reducible to ∅⁽ᵐ⁾ for some m.

nodes.name: Piling-up lemma
nodes.statement: For independent binary random variables X₁, …, Xₙ, the imbalance P(X=0) − P(X=1) of their XOR equals the product of the imbalances of the individual variables. Equivalently, the bias P(X=0) − 1/2 of the XOR equals 2ⁿ⁻¹ times the product of the individual biases.
nodes.by: Introduced by Mitsuru Matsui, 1993
nodes.note: It is used in linear cryptanalysis to build linear approximations to the action of block ciphers.

nodes.name: Chomsky–Schützenberger representation theorem
nodes.statement: A language L over the alphabet Σ is context-free if and only if there exist a matched alphabet T ∪ T̄, a regular language R over T ∪ T̄, and a homomorphism h from (T ∪ T̄)* to Σ* such that L = h(D_T ∩ R), where D_T is the Dyck language of correctly nested sequences over the matched alphabet.
nodes.by: Noam Chomsky and Marcel-Paul Schützenberger, 1959
nodes.note: Every context-free language is obtained from a Dyck language by intersecting with a regular language and applying a homomorphism.

nodes.name: Linear speedup theorem
nodes.statement: For any real c > 0 and any Turing machine with k > 1 tapes that solves a problem in time f(n), there is another k-tape Turing machine that solves the same problem in time at most f(n)/c + 2n + 3.
nodes.note: The new machine gets its speed by using a larger tape alphabet. If the original machine is non-deterministic, so is the new one.

nodes.name: Myhill–Nerode theorem
nodes.statement: For a language L, call two strings x and y equivalent if there is no string z such that exactly one of xz and yz belongs to L. Then L is regular if and only if this relation has finitely many equivalence classes; that number then equals the number of states of the minimal deterministic finite automaton accepting L, and every minimal such automaton is isomorphic to the canonical one built from these classes.
nodes.by: John Myhill and Anil Nerode, 1957
nodes.note: Its corollary that a language with infinitely many equivalence classes is not regular is frequently used to prove that a language is not regular.

nodes.name: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
nodes.statement: Any two NP-complete languages are p-isomorphic: there is a one-to-one correspondence between strings that sends members of one language exactly to members of the other, such that both the correspondence and its inverse can be computed in polynomial time.
nodes.by: Leonard C. Berman and Juris Hartmanis
nodes.note: If true, there would be no sparse NP-complete languages, which would imply P ≠ NP. Many complexity theorists believe the conjecture is false.

nodes.name: Compression theorem
nodes.statement: Fix a Gödel numbering φ of the computable functions and a Blum complexity measure Φ, and for a function f let C(f) be the class of total computable functions φᵢ whose complexity Φᵢ(x) is at most f(x) for all but finitely many x. Then there is a total computable function f such that for every i, φᵢ and φ_f(i) have the same domain and C(φᵢ) is strictly contained in C(φ_f(i)).
nodes.note: Consequently there is no largest complexity class with computable boundary that contains all computable functions.

nodes.name: Courcelle's theorem
nodes.statement: Every graph property definable in the monadic second-order logic of graphs can be decided in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth.
nodes.by: Bruno Courcelle, 1990; independently rediscovered by Borie and Parker and Tovey, 1992
nodes.note: It is considered the archetype of algorithmic meta-theorems.

nodes.name: Forking lemma
nodes.statement: Let A be a probabilistic algorithm with random tape r that takes input (x, h₁, …, h_q; r), where x is drawn from a distribution IG and each hᵢ is drawn uniformly from a set H of size h, and that outputs a pair (J, y) with J one of 0, 1, …, q; let acc be the probability that J ≥ 1. The forking algorithm runs A, and if J ≥ 1 runs it again with the same x, r and h₁, …, h_{J−1} but fresh random values for positions J to q, and it succeeds if the second run returns the same J and the new J-th value differs from h_J; the probability frk of success satisfies frk ≥ acc·(acc/q − 1/h).
nodes.by: First used by David Pointcheval and Jacques Stern, Eurocrypt 1996; later generalized by Mihir Bellare and Gregory Neven
nodes.note: It is used to prove the security of digital signature schemes and other constructions based on random oracles. The reduction it provides is not tight.

nodes.name: Gottesman–Knill theorem
nodes.statement: A quantum circuit that uses only preparation of qubits in computational-basis states, Clifford gates (generated by the Hadamard, controlled NOT and phase gates) and measurements in the computational basis can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer. Such stabilizer circuits can be simulated perfectly in polynomial time on a probabilistic classical computer.
nodes.by: Daniel Gottesman and Emanuel Knill
nodes.note: It shows that even some highly entangled states can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer. It was published in a single-author paper by Gottesman, who credits Knill with the result.

nodes.name: Karp–Lipton theorem
nodes.statement: If the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) can be solved by Boolean circuits with a polynomial number of logic gates, then Π₂ = Σ₂ and therefore the polynomial hierarchy PH equals Σ₂.
nodes.by: Richard M. Karp and Richard J. Lipton, 1980; Michael Sipser improved the collapse from Σ₃ to Σ₂
nodes.note: Such a collapse is believed unlikely, so the theorem is viewed as evidence that SAT and other NP-complete problems have no polynomial size circuits.

nodes.name: Leftover hash lemma
nodes.statement: Let X be a random variable with min-entropy H(X) = −log maxₓ Pr[X = x], let m > 0, and let h(S, X) be a 2-universal hash function with values in {0,1}ᵐ. If m ≤ H(X) − 2 log(1/ε), then for S uniform and independent of X, the statistical distance between (h(S, X), S) and (U, S) is at most ε, where U is uniform on {0,1}ᵐ and independent of S.
nodes.by: First stated by Russell Impagliazzo, Leonid Levin, and Michael Luby
nodes.note: It means that a key about which an adversary knows only part can be turned into a shorter key that is almost uniformly random for the adversary. This is also known as privacy amplification.

nodes.name: Low basis theorem
nodes.statement: Every nonempty Π⁰₁ class in 2^ω contains a set of low degree, that is, a set whose Turing jump is Turing equivalent to the halting problem ∅′. Equivalently, every infinite computable subtree of the binary tree 2^{<ω} has an infinite path of low degree.
nodes.note: It is one of several basis theorems, which find paths with particular computability properties through infinite subtrees of the binary tree. It implies the existence of PA degrees strictly below ∅′.

nodes.name: Arden's rule
nodes.statement: For sets of strings A and B, the set A*⋅B is the smallest language X satisfying X = A⋅X ∪ B, and if A does not contain the empty word, this solution is unique. Equivalently, B⋅A* is the smallest solution of X = X⋅A ∪ B.
nodes.note: It can be used to help convert some finite automata to regular expressions, as in Kleene's algorithm.

nodes.name: Toda's theorem
nodes.statement: The entire polynomial hierarchy PH is contained in P^PP. It follows that PH is also contained in P^#P.
nodes.by: Seinosuke Toda
nodes.note: The result was given the 1998 Gödel Prize.

nodes.name: Rice–Shapiro theorem
nodes.statement: Let P be a set of partial computable functions such that the set of program indices e with φ_e in P, for a fixed admissible numbering φ, is semi-decidable. Then for every partial computable function f, P contains f if and only if P contains a finite subfunction of f, that is, a function defined at only finitely many points that agrees with f there.
nodes.by: Named after Henry Gordon Rice and Norman Shapiro
nodes.note: It generalizes Rice's theorem. A closely related result is the Kreisel–Lacombe–Shoenfield–Tseitin theorem.

nodes.name: Schaefer's dichotomy theorem
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a finite set of relations over the Boolean domain {0, 1}. The constraint satisfaction problem CSP(Γ) is solvable in polynomial time if Γ has one of six polymorphisms: the constant 1, the constant 0, binary AND, binary OR, ternary majority, or ternary minority (x ⊕ y ⊕ z); otherwise it is NP-complete. An operation is a polymorphism of Γ if applying it coordinate-wise to tuples of any relation in Γ always gives a tuple of that relation.
nodes.by: Thomas Jerome Schaefer
nodes.note: Special cases include the NP-completeness of SAT, 1-in-3 SAT and not-all-equal 3SAT, also in their monotone versions.

nodes.name: Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem
nodes.statement: For any function s(n) ≥ log n, the class of problems solvable by a nondeterministic machine in space s(n) equals the class of complements of such problems, that is NSPACE(s(n)) = co-NSPACE(s(n)). The special case s(n) = log n is NL = co-NL.
nodes.by: Neil Immerman and Róbert Szelepcsényi, independently, 1987
nodes.note: No similar result is known for time complexity classes. The theorem solved the second LBA problem, and its proof method is called inductive counting.

nodes.name: Sipser–Lautemann theorem
nodes.statement: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time (BPP) is contained in the polynomial time hierarchy, and more specifically in Σ₂ ∩ Π₂.
nodes.by: Michael Sipser, 1983, showed that BPP is in the polynomial hierarchy; Péter Gács showed that it is in Σ₂ ∩ Π₂; Clemens Lautemann gave a simple proof of this, also in 1983
nodes.note: It is conjectured that BPP = P, which is a much stronger statement.

nodes.name: Space hierarchy theorem
nodes.statement: Call a function f from the natural numbers to the natural numbers space-constructible if f(n) ≥ log n and some Turing machine, started on a string of n ones, computes f(n) using space O(f(n)). For every space-constructible f there is a language that can be decided in space O(f(n)) but not in space o(f(n)), so SPACE(g(n)) is a proper subset of SPACE(f(n)) for every g(n) in o(f(n)), for deterministic and for nondeterministic machines alike.
nodes.note: The theorem is false if f is not required to be space-constructible. The analogous time hierarchy theorems are somewhat weaker.

nodes.name: UTM theorem
nodes.statement: There is a partial computable function u of two variables such that for every computable function f of one variable there is a number e with f(x) ≃ u(e,x) for all x. This means that for each x, either f(x) and u(e,x) are both defined and equal, or both are undefined.
nodes.note: The function u is called a universal function. It is an abstract version of the universal Turing machine.

nodes.name: Valiant–Vazirani theorem
nodes.statement: If there is a polynomial time algorithm for Unambiguous-SAT, then NP = RP. Unambiguous-SAT is the problem of deciding, for a Boolean formula that has at most one satisfying assignment, whether it is unsatisfiable or has exactly one satisfying assignment.
nodes.by: Leslie Valiant and Vijay Vazirani, 1986
nodes.note: It implies that Boolean satisfiability remains computationally hard even when the inputs are promised to have at most one satisfying assignment.

nodes.name: Savitch's theorem
nodes.statement: For any space-constructable function f with f ∈ Ω(log n), every problem solvable by a nondeterministic Turing machine in space f(n) is solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in space f(n)². That is, NSPACE(f(n)) ⊆ DSPACE(f(n)²).
nodes.by: Walter Savitch, 1970
nodes.note: It shows that nondeterminism has a much more limited effect on space requirements than it appears to have on time. The theorem still holds when every Turing machine is replaced by an oracle Turing machine.

nodes.name: Hilbert's tenth problem
nodes.statement: There is no general algorithm that, for every Diophantine equation (a polynomial equation with integer coefficients and a finite number of unknowns), decides whether the equation has a solution in which all unknowns are integers.
nodes.by: Posed by David Hilbert, 1900; solved in the negative by Martin Davis, Yuri Matiyasevich, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson over 21 years, with Matiyasevich completing the theorem in 1970
nodes.note: The question was posed by David Hilbert in 1900 as the tenth problem on his list. Its negative answer follows from the MRDP theorem, which says that every recursively enumerable set is Diophantine.
